speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: INTERNATIONAL WOMEN'S YEAR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as this session of parliament reconvenes, we are entering not only a new year-and I hope it will be a happy one for all hon. members-but a unique and special period, International Women's Year.

subsubtopic: INTERNATIONAL WOMEN'S YEAR
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Trudeau:
subsubtopic: INTERNATIONAL WOMEN'S YEAR
speechtext:
International Women's Year, 1975, was proclaimed by the United Nations. It is a year which has three goals: peace, development and equality. Canada, as a member nation, has undertaken a substantial program of support for this special year, through legislation, through funding of groups and organizations, through the promotion of equality within federal government departments and agencies, and through the promotion of a national awareness of the current status of women.

One of the most evident means the government has at its disposal to improve the status of women is through legislation. Parliament is considering at this time an
omnibus bill on the status of women which aims at amending eight federal statutes. Thanks to this bill, the government will be able to eliminate sections which, in various statutes, discriminate against women. Other legislative amendments are also being considered: one of them will bring about the establishment of a federal commission of human rights.
We are very happy to have nine women sit with us in the House, an unprecedented number. Because of their sex, we are inclined to look upon these hon. members as official spokesmen on every topic related to the status of women, which is quite understandable. Yet, there are 264 hon. members altogether in Parliament, and each and every one of these men and women should lend an ear to the demands of women: do they not make up half of the electorate? The status of women is a national problem which must be of interest to all Canadian men and women.
Discrimination against women is in some ways comparable to discrimination against society's other disadvantaged groups. It is not always overt. In fact, as both provincial and federal governments work to introduce legislation that provides equal rights in many areas, the acts of discrimination themselves often become more subtle and insidious. The crucial and necessary changes are frequently required in areas where no legislation can ever be introduced-in attitudes. Yet it is attitudes that often militate against equal treatment for women and men.
During International Women's Year it is hoped that all the people of Canada will work toward making equality a reality by truly recognizing women and men as equals. Real freedom of opportunity for women will come when society recognizes that women have the same right to pursue whatever goals they may individually choose, be that goal centred on home and family or career or a combination of any such goals. This equality of opportunity can only come about when all Canadians recognize women as full and equal contributors to our society.
International Women's Year is a year in which we can acknowledge the major contributions which women have made to Canada's social, cultural, political and economic development. It is also a time to ensure that as women choose new roles, the doorways are opened so that they may continue to make such contributions.
It would, however, be unrealistic to assume that full equality will be achieved in just one year. It is for this reason that International Women's Year, while being a special year, must not be regarded as an end in itself but must be seen in the context of the government's ongoing program to improve the status of women. This work must

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: INTERNATIONAL WOMEN'S YEAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to associate myself and my colleagues with the marking of the commencement of International Women's Year proclaimed by the United Nations. I hope that we will see, during 1975, not only happy members of parliament, as referred to by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), but very marked progress in the achievement of equality for women in this country and in other countries as well.
Opportunities for careers for women in our country are unquestionably expanding. We must, however, recognize that we are still behind some countries, some societies with regard to the position of women in our society, opportunities for women, and their equality. While it may be that there are now very few careers really closed to women, I think any man would have to admit that in Canada there are many careers in which a women has to be considerably abler, smarter and more industrious than a man in order to succeed.
If we look around us here today, without casting any aspersions upon the qualities or intelligence of those of the same sex as myself I would have to admit that the Commons as it presently exists is not truly representative of this country, in the sense that women are not adequately represented.

subsubtopic: INTERNATIONAL WOMEN'S YEAR
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanfield:
subsubtopic: INTERNATIONAL WOMEN'S YEAR
speechtext: I probably have to admit, too, that the women who are here had to be a good deal more able, better politicians than me in order to get here. I am surprised that that comment did not receive a great deal of applause, at least from across the way. In any case, let us hope that 1975 will be a productive year in terms of improvement in the status of women, particularly in our own country, because it is in our own country, for which we have responsibility, that we need definite programs. I rather suspect that women in Canada are not now particularly interested in conferences and commissions; they want to see definite, tangible changes and improvements.

subsubtopic: INTERNATIONAL WOMEN'S YEAR
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanfield:
subsubtopic: INTERNATIONAL WOMEN'S YEAR
speechtext:
It is now three or four years since the report on the status of women was tabled in this House. Many of its recommendations still have not been carried out. We must recognize that it is more difficult for a woman in Canada, generally speaking, to achieve an equal place in the world of work than it is for a man. While I would not expect even this government to overcome this difficulty completely in one year, let us hope we see some significant progress in very tangible ways, Mr. Speaker.
Some bon. Members: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Broadbent:
subsubtopic: INTERNATIONAL WOMEN'S YEAR
speechtext:
The catcalls are even more incoherent than usual, Mr. Speaker. The point is a serious one. If we are making statements on important social questions, members of the opposition, the Leader of the Opposition and myself should receive substantially more notification than we did today. That is all I am going to say on this issue.
Mr. Speaker, on this important human and social question the time has passed for conferences, commissions and slick advertising campaigns. The women of Canada, like women all over the western industrial world, now see themselves, appropriately, as being in a moral, social and economic sense subject to the will of others. It is, speaking quite frankly, a male reaction-and I am part of that reaction-to steps taken by the women of this country and others that is finally, and reluctantly, leading to legislative, social and economic change that will provide real equality for women.
Let us not be under any illusion-and I direct these comments to the women of Canada-that if they want real change and real progress, they will have to keep the heat on this House of Commons and on other legislative bodies. No social group in our history, or in the history of any other country, has had their liberation made for them by others. They get it when they create pressure and force on society to get those with authority and influence to make the necessary changes. I want, in a very specific way, to make ten very brief points.

speakeroldname: Mr. Broadbent:
subsubtopic: INTERNATIONAL WOMEN'S YEAR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would very much welcome your cutting me off after I have used the same amount of time as the Prime Minister.

subsubtopic: INTERNATIONAL WOMEN'S YEAR
speechtext: Shame.

speakeroldname: Mr. Broadbent:
subsubtopic: INTERNATIONAL WOMEN'S YEAR
speechtext:
I would suggest, with respect, Mr. Speaker, that I can make ten points in the time that he took to make none. It is a measure of the lack of equality in this country that the following ten points can still be called for at this time:
First, laws are required prohibiting discrimination because of sex or marital status in the recruitment, classification, promotion, dismissal and advertising of jobs in Canada. They do not exist.
Second, we need child-care centres for children of all ages which are free, community controlled and available on a 24-hour a day basis.
Third, tough laws, strictly enforced, are needed to provide equal pay for work of equal value and to provide incentives to achieve this objective.
Fourth, changes in labour laws are required to provide collective bargaining rights and fringe benefits for domestic and part-time workers. Women in our society find themselves, much more than men, in the category of parttime workers.
Fifth, we need amendments to pension laws to give all women, including those who work at home, the same rights to join and to draw benefits as are enjoyed by men.
Sixth, we need effective guarantees that male and female students are equally entitled to enroll-and I mean effectively equally entitled-in any course of their choosing so that vocations in our society will be equally available to both sexes.
Seventh, we need the elimination, particularly at the elementary school level, of sex stereotyping in text-books. All of us know the kind of examples which could be cited that prevail in our textbooks.
Eighth, we need action taken against advertising which exploits sex and demeans the role and place of women in society.
Ninth, amendments are needed to take abortion out of the Criminal Code so that women are free to act in accordance with their consciences and on the advice of a qualified medical expert.
Tenth, we need the establishment of sex education and birth control centres adequately equipped to advise on family planning, birth control methods, abortion, pre-natal and post-natal care, and ways and means of caring for and supporting a child in the case of an unplanned pregnancy.
Mr. Speaker, those are my ten brief points. Much more could be added but I will conclude with what I said at the
Prime Minister's Swimming Pool
outset: the time for conferences has passed and the time for action is upon us.

subsubtopic: INTERNATIONAL WOMEN'S YEAR
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Real Caouette (Temiscamingue):
subsubtopic: INTERNATIONAL WOMEN'S YEAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleagues and I are happy to join the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Leaders of the Official Opposition and of the New Democratic Party in wishing International Women's Year all the success anticipated by this organization.
As the Prime Minister said a moment ago, we are happy to have with us, in this Parliament, women who represent the voters from their respective constituencies.
I believe that the presence of women enhances the quality of the Canadian Parliament. We feel, and I am convinced, that women must fully play their role in our society, whether in the parliamentary, family or business fields and that they are entitled to respect. Mr. Speaker, I also say that women must never be slaves in any society or organization. In some parts of the world, women are on an equal footing with men. For instance, when I was in Russia, I saw women coming out of coal mines. I would not be happy to see a woman working at the Noranda's mine in my own riding, but rather a woman well respected in her own situation. I do not know how the leaders of other parties have organized the political activity of their offices, but in the Social Credit Party leader's office the executive is a woman and she carries out a very important job. All members are in a position to note the efficiency of their office secretary and also to treat equally their male and female employees.
Mr. Speaker, a moment ago the Prime Minister was right to offer his best wishes for International Women's Year, and so do my colleagues and I, not in order that women be better than men, but that they be treated equally throughout Canada.

subsubtopic: TAX FREE BONDS
speechtext:
1.	Has the government rejected the introduction of tax free bonds and, if so, for what reasons?
2.	Will the government consider tax changes to facilitate the issuance by municipalities of tax free bonds?

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance):
subsubtopic: TAX FREE BONDS
speechtext:
At the
present time the government does not intend to introduce tax free bonds for the following reasons: 1. In a tax system such as ours, based on graduated rates of taxation the use of tax free bonds would primarily benefit upper income taxpayers, because a non-inclusion in taxable income is more valuable to taxpayers who would otherwise be required to pay a greater proportion of their income in the form of tax. Such a result would introduce unfairness into the income tax system.
2. There is a tendency to overestimate the extent to which a tax exemption for interest would enable municipalities to borrow money at lower rates of interest. The tax exempt feature would not attract tax exempt purchasers such as pension plans or charitable foundations and therefore the market for these bonds would be restricted. Finally, the increased competition caused by the entry of tax free bonds might cause confusion in the capital markets and cause a rise in interest rates on taxable bonds in

January 22, 1975

order to attract investors. Such a result would add to the current inflationary trends in the economy. For these reasons the government is now not considering proposing tax changes to facilitate the issuance by municipalities of tax free bonds.

subsubtopic: EXPROPRIATION OF SMALL BUSINESS PROPERTY
speechtext:
1.	When a government department expropriates a small business property which provides the only source of income for the owner, is it prepared to recognize that the price which the owner is awarded will not set him up in business in a new and perhaps unsuitable locality, nor will it replace his building?
2.	Is the government prepared to consider the plight of a person who runs a store or business dependent on local trade who is, from a practical point of view, compelled to accept the price established by the government, since it would be necessary to give up his business if he chose to fight the delays and frustrations of dealing with a bureaucracy and different agencies?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: EXPROPRIATION OF SMALL BUSINESS PROPERTY
speechtext:
1. Under the New Expropriation Act (Chapter 16 RSC 1970), Section 24 of the said Act sets the rules for determining value. When the Crown expropriates a small business whereby the owner operates out of his own building, the said owner will be paid the market value which is determined as follows: (a) the market value determined on the basis that the use to which the expropriated interest was being put at the time of its taking, was its highest and best use, plus (b) the costs, expenses and losses arising out of or incidental to the owner's disturbance including moving to other premises or, if those costs cannot be estimated, an amount not to exceed 15 per cent of the market value determined in (a), plus (c) any value to the owner representing a special economic advantage to him arising out of or incidental to his occupation of the land, to the extent that no provision was made in (a) and (b) above. With regard to the relocation itself, it is the owner's responsibility to find a location where he can continue his business.
2. Under Section 14(1) (b) of the New Expropriation Act (Chapter 16 RSC 1970), the Minister shall, within 90 days after the Notice of Confirmation has been registered, make an offer in writing to the expropriated interest. Such offer is equal to the full amount which, in the opinion of
January 22, 1975

the Minister, represents his interest in the property being expropriated. He can accept the amount without prejudice to the right of claiming additional compensation. Such right is valid for one year after he accepted the original offer. Such procedure allows him to avoid the delays and frustrations of dealing with a bureaucracy.

Has the Government of the United States recognized in writing the absolute, unfettered, untrammelled and unqualified right of the government to regulate every aspect whatsoever of movement, commerce, access, shipping, exploration, exploitation and industry in those islands and the waters surrounding them, commonly referred to as the Canadian Arctic Archipelago, as if such land, water and ice were part of territorial Canada, and (a) if so, is the government prepared to make this document public (b) if not, for what reason?
January 22, 1975

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There has been no written communication from the United States government with respect to the matters raised in the question. At the time of the enactment of the Arctic Waters Pollution Prevention Act in April of 1970 the United States Department of State issued a press release concerning Canada's claim to jurisdiction over Arctic pollution. That press release was published as "Appendix A" to the Hansard of April 15, 1970. The Canadian government replied to the United States position with a diplomatic note which was handed to the United States government on April 16, 1970. A summary of that note appeared as an appendix to the Hansard of April 17, 1970. The Canadian government maintains the views it expressed at that time.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION ON LIFTING OF FREIGHT RATE FREEZE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Transport.
The 18-month freeze period applicable to rail freight rates had been initiated at the Western Economic Opportunities Conference, supposedly to give the government time to formulate a new and more equitable transport policy. Is the minister reconsidering his support of the freeze suspension, since no new policy has come up during the last 18 months?

speakeroldname: Hon. dean Marchand (Minister of Transport):
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION ON LIFTING OF FREIGHT RATE FREEZE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. Leader of the Opposition will refer to Hansard, he will see that our request to the two railway companies not to raise their prices was made before the conference in the west. It was not related to the conference of Calgary, but we made it to the railway companies in order to make an example, because the pressure of inflation was beginning to be felt.
As regards the effect of our request, Mr. Speaker, we were able to analize it afterwards. Of course, during the following months, we realized that that accounted for only 22 per cent of the revenue of the railway companies. The rates that were provided for by contract, the rates that were agreed on with shippers, were in no way affected by the agreement that had been made, and that created an important distortion with the rates established by the trucking companies.
In the circumstances, Mr. Speaker, and since we had made a commitment that the freeze would last only until December 31, I think that policy was not a real policy, but only an example the government wanted to give the Canadian people. If we want a price freeze policy, it will have to be global, and not cover only 22 per cent, but 100 per cent of the economy, not only of the railway rates, but

of other prices also. That is what Canadian voters rejected later on.

Mr. Speaker, my question is supplementary to that of the Leader of the Opposition to the Minister of Transport
January 22, 1975

Oral Questions CONSUMER AFFAIRS
having to do with LCL rates. In view of the fact that the removal of LCL rates to the Atlantic region, and particularly Newfoundland, will create hardship to small businesses and increase costs, resulting in increased costs to the consumer, would the minister direct CNR to reconsider the removal of LCL rates and reinitiate them only when he has a chance to come up with the program which he mentioned in the reply to the Leader of the Opposition?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Marchand (Minister of Transport):
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED MAINTENANCE OF LCL FREIGHT RATES UNTIL NEW POLICY ANNOUNCED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I made a commitment to the ministers of transport of the Atlantic provinces, including the minister in charge of transport for Newfoundland. We want to know exactly which sector is affected because the freeze affected only 22 per cent of the commodities moved. We want to know exactly who is affected because, as the hon. member knows very well, this freeze has been a real windfall for certain groups and it did result in increased prices even though the rates were frozen. So, we do not want to apply a blanket freeze at this moment. We want to study each case and we are committed to that. The federal-provincial committee on transportation will make a study, and if anyone is really seriously affected, we will take measures to protect him.

speechtext: My question is directed to the minister responsible for fisheries. It concerns the deepsea fishermen's strike now taking place in Newfoundland. speakeroldname: Hon. Romeo LeBlanc (Minister of State (Fisheries)):
subsubtopic: POSSIBLE USE OF TWENTY MILLION DOLLAR FUND TO IMPLEMENT HARRIS REPORT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the allocation of money was to help the industry over a difficult period, and helping the industry meant keeping the fishery going. Part of this money was, of course, intended to affect the price for fish paid to fishermen.

subsubtopic: POSSIBLE USE OF TWENTY MILLION DOLLAR FUND TO IMPLEMENT HARRIS REPORT-GOVERNMENT POSITION

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR OUTLINE OF NEW POLICY
speechtext:

He said that the new transportation policy, which he said in Halifax was going to be related to a new deal for economic development of the Atlantic region, will not now be ready until April or May.

January 22, 1975

speechtext: Notwithstanding the negative and infantile reaction of certain members of the opposition, we are working very hard on the transportation policy. Many people are working on this. I hope that we are going to find the solution to the problem which, incidentally has not been found by any government, least of all those in opposition who at one time formed the government. There are some elements of solution, but we have no over-all policy, and this is what we have-

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs. I am not yet in a position to release the agenda of the meeting with housing ministers, but naturally it is going to be directed at the groups benefitting from the implementation of those programs for which they show a considerable amount of enthusiasm, continuing interest and alertness

with respect to the housing situation with which we are all concerned.

speakeroldname: Miss Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince Albert):
subsubtopic: LAVELLE CASE-SUGGESTED REMOVAL FROM LAW OF DISCRIMINATION AGAINST INDIAN WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was the disinterest of the hon. gentlemen in anything but abortion that caused me to ask that question,
I therefore direct a supplementary question to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I refer him to the Lavelle case, an extraordinary judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada last fall in which the majority of the judges, with the chief justice dissenting, came to a
January 22, 1975

conclusion that Indian Women were not entitled to the same rights as male Indians. Will the minister have that injustice removed so that we can take one step along the road to assuring women equal rights and make a great many of the platitudes that have been uttered here as to the affection for women and need of them having equal rights, come about?

subsubtopic: LAVELLE CASE-SUGGESTED REMOVAL FROM LAW OF DISCRIMINATION AGAINST INDIAN WOMEN
speechtext: Yes or no?

speakeroldname: Hon. Judd Buchanan (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: LAVELLE CASE-SUGGESTED REMOVAL FROM LAW OF DISCRIMINATION AGAINST INDIAN WOMEN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, an undertaking was given to all Indian people in Canada that the federal government would not unilaterally alter the Indian Act without consultation with the Indian people. They have given us preliminary proposals, amongst which is a clause providing that the discriminatory aspect be removed in the sense that neither a male or female spouse, on marrying an Indian person, would acquire Indian status, nor would any offspring. They made it clear that that was a tentative proposal and asked us to bide our time until they consulted with all the Indian people before they made a final representation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Diefenbaker:
subsubtopic: LAVELLE CASE-SUGGESTED REMOVAL FROM LAW OF DISCRIMINATION AGAINST INDIAN WOMEN
speechtext: Not necessarily not discrimination, but discrimination if necessary.

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance) moved
speechtext: that Bill C-39, to amend the Customs Tariff (No. 2), be read the second time and referred to committee of the whole.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Cullen (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset may I thank the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) for the courtesy extended to the minister in enabling him to attend an important meeting today and for the courtesy extended to me in enabling me to introduce this bill on second reading.
The bill before us reintroduces a number of the temporary tariff reductions initially introduced in the February, 1973, budget. Those reductions formed an important part of the comprehensive program contained in that budget. Then, as now, the two-fold thrust of the budget was to provide continuing stimulus to economic growth and at the same time mitigate inflationary pressures. It is believed that these reductions can play an important part on the anti-inflationary side of our two-pronged attack on the problems facing the Canadian economy.
The tariff reductions in the February, 1973, budget covered a wide range of food and non-food products. They remained in effect for an initial period of one year and were subsequently continued for most of the products until June 30, 1974. In the May 6 budget it was proposed that they be extended to December 31, 1974. In the preparation of the November budget the minister reviewed this group of reductions and decided that a large proportion of them should be put back in place and for a longer period, until June 30, 1976, as set out in clause 3(2) of the bill. However, as he said in his budget speech, because of the longer period during which they will be in effect, compared with the shorter period suggested in May, because of the introduction on July 1 of the general preferential tariff for imports from developing countries, and because of certain changed price and supply circumstances about which the minister has received representations, we are proposing a number of exclusions from the May list of reductions.
With the slowdown in construction both in Canada and the United States, particularly the reduced number of housing starts, some products, the demand for which is related to housing starts, have been left out of the present package of tariff reductions. These include plywood, furniture, white goods, house trailers and mobile homes. A
Customs Tariff
number of other products have been left out because competition in our market has been affected by the introduction on July 1, 1974, of the general preferential tariff for imports from those developing countries which have been designated as beneficiaries of that tariff. In this group are batteries, luggage, and toys.
As hon. members are aware, general preferential tariff rates are the lower of the existing British preferential tariff rates or the most favoured nation tariff rates reduced by one-third. To prevent the tariff reductions proposed in the bill from automatically resulting in further reductions in these rates, the bill provides that the current GPT rates will not be altered by the present measure. In the food sector, a number of products such as live hogs, fresh lamb and mutton, fresh pork and other meat products have been left out of the present proposal because of the current difficult market situation for meats.
Tariff reductions on a number of products included in the February, 1973, budget had the effect of reducing or eliminating margins of preference which are bound into our trade agreement with Australia. By "margins of preference" I mean the difference between the rates which apply under the most favoured nation tariff and those which apply on imports from Australia. In the present bill it is proposed that the British preferential rate on meat extracts be reduced to free in order to preserve the margin of preference on Australian exports. Also excluded from the present measure are raisins and currants which are important Australian exports to our country. In return for the margins of tariff preference we maintain for Australia, we receive important trade preferences in that market.
A few other food products were excluded to meet specific problems encountered by Canadian producers. While every effort was made to avoid adverse effects on production and employment in Canada, sudden market reversals in other sectors of our economy could very well occur between now and June 30, 1976. For this reason, the minister is again asking parliament to give authority to the government to restore the pre-budget rates of duty on any particular product or group of products where maintenance of the reduction could result in genuine hardship.
The bill also includes a number of other provisions originally included in the May 6 budget. Undoubtedly, the most important of these, from the general public's point of view, is the substantial increase in the so-called tourist exemptions. Canadians claimed about four million exemptions in 1973, and in that year over $110 million worth of goods were allowed duty and tax free entry under these provisions. We are frequently asked why the tourist exemption is not increased to an even higher level, say to the $100 a month allowance for American tourists. The purpose of our tourist exemption is to enable Canadian travellers abroad to bring back from their holidays, free of duty and taxes, a quantity of goods and souvenirs which the average tourist might hope to purchase incidental to his trip.
With a large proportion of the Canadian population living within 100 miles of the Canada-U.S. border, and with lower retail prices in the United States due to three

January 22, 1975
Customs Tariff
measures, differences in taxation, the greater range of products available, and the effect of spill-over advertising, there would be a strong incentive to undertake shopping excursions if the Canadian exemptions for a 48-hour absence were substantially higher than is now proposed. I might say it is our estimate that our much smaller population spends about as much on shopping in the United States as American tourists spend here.
Another important item in this group is that which will provide authority for the government to allow duty free entry on bona fide handicraft products from developing countries. Because of the difficulty in defining precisely what are handicraft products, we felt that some discretion should be left to the government to ensure that our own craftsmen would not be adversely affected by too broad an interpretation of what constitutes handicraft products.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Lambert (Edmonton West):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, debate on any stage of a bill amending the Customs Tariff has about the lowest public appeal of any subject. On the other hand, the debate that will follow on continuation of the consideration of Bill C-40, which is to amend the Excise Tax Act, will bring forward many representations from my colleagues. I trust that those who received representations during the Christmas recess will put them before the parliamentary secretary or the minister tomorrow.
Unless there has been a major accord, as there was under the Kennedy round, and which may come forward some years hence when the Tokyo talks are completed and countries have come to some form of agreement with regard to further tariff modifications, we will have a considerably sized volume for the Customs Tariff. If one refers to the consolidated Statutes of Canada to find the Customs Tariff, one is faced with a bewildering array of columns of figures and items. There is descriptive language which possesses unto itself the reputation of that which has been more narrowly construed than any other language of government statute or regulation. We may consider some of these this afternoon.
The parliamentary secretary, on behalf of the minister, has indicated that the items included in this amendment to the Customs Tariff were considered in the preparation of the budget about a year ago to be conducive to fighting inflation. The government did not seem to be so aware of inflation a year ago. I do not know if these particular items, chosen for fighting inflation at this time, were stated to be for the same purpose at that time. Frankly, I do not think any of them are designed to fight inflation.
This amendment will result in a reduction of tax. Hopefully, it will reduce either the price or the pressure for a potential price increase. As far as the Canadian citizen is concerned, he will be affected mostly by increased simplification of the provisions regarding allowances for tourists returning after an absence from Canada. To that extent there has been a simplification. However, the change to $150 from $100, and to $50 from $25 is nothing more than recognition of the degree of inflation that has taken place in the past two years. Therefore, in so far as the Canadian tourist is concerned, he cannot buy abroad, quantitatively, any more today than he did five years ago. I know this from personal experience. As a matter of fact, I had this experience in the past week and saw the effect.

Within the past year or so I have had occasion to return to Canada from abroad three times. When my wife and I returned from the Far East about a year ago, we had acquired gifts for the family. We found it exceedingly difficult to buy anything and not go over the top. On a modest amount of purchases, mostly from Commonwealth countries and all from developing countries, we exceeded the limit and had to pay a fair amount of duty.
I hope this question will be kept under active review. It is part of the move between countries. The United States asked us to do this in the past and they increased the amount American citizens could bring back from abroad. That was a good move. If we are to spend many thousands of dollars to encourage tourists to come here, there must be a corresponding gesture on our part. As we know, Canadians are great travellers. They spend their money abroad, encouraging international trade in that way.
I wish to make a second point. I hope the minister will be able to answer this question at third reading. In fact, he indicated in informal discussions that he would do so. I realize these questions would be better directed to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) since they deal with the forthcoming GATT negotiations in Tokyo. I understand that the technical staffs have been informed and there has been some difficulty. I would have thought it would have been far better for the Government of Canada to name not only departmental officials to these negotiating bodies but also some practical businessmen.
There has always been a great deal of resentment, as there was at the time of the Kennedy round, that these negotiations were, frankly, some sort of "in" club proposition among the bureaucrats of the departments of finance, industry, trade and commerce, or what have you, of the countries represented in the negotiations. So far as Canada is concerned, one could not get any idea of what was being done; they were as close mouthed as anything. I know that this is a trading game and it usually turns out to be an item-for-item exchange. In many instances, in order to gain a point you have to kill off a couple of Canadian industries or something. A number of industries were badly hurt-fine papers, chemicals, and so on-at the time of the Kennedy round, but I think a great deal more openness and frankness with industry within this country would be of benefit so far as further negotiations on sweeping tariff changes are concerned.
I think we are all generally seeking to improve international trade. We have to do something particularly with the third world countries. I do not know what the answer is. Certainly there is no simplistic answer. It is not a question of the developed countries having to close down their industries and transfer them to the developing countries. That is not going to work. For one thing, the trained personnel are not there, there is adaptability to climate and too many complications of that sort. Frankly, I have never been impressed with arguments from some developing countries that deliberate closing down of industries should take place in the developed countries so they can be transferred to the developing countries.
It seems to me that much greater efforts should be turned toward developing, with expert help, indigenous

industries in the particular countries for which they are best suited. Then we could make the necessary trade and price adjustments with respect to the commodities produced. Frankly, we have introduced a special line of tariffs, which is merely a structure that includes no barriers, regarding many goods emanating from developing countries. If we are in some way to alleviate some of the problems that have arisen as a result of the worldly imbalance of trade caused by the energy crisis last year, which imbalance is still continuing, then we must be one of the nations, I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, in the vanguard pressing for wide, sweeping negotiations to revise trading patterns, thus restoring some balance and alleviating the problems of many countries. It is not only the third world countries that are facing difficulties; many established economies have been especially hard hit. Thus, it is nonsense to continue with the patterns that have developed.
I think it is unfortunate that we shall see a succession of OPEC-type situations which will result in, not a form of nationalism by one country but, rather, a form of product nationalism by a group of countries who will try to arrogate unto themselves a greater and greater share of the world's economy in some sort of wild scramble. We are seeing this situation developing in sugar and in coffee, and we will see it in cocoa and in bauxite. We have seen what has happened to petroleum. The list may be endless. It then becomes jungle warfare and GATT agreements are just tossed out of the window. As a matter of fact, I am wondering how far the OPEC agreements would stand up to real scrutiny under GATT, if anyone had the desire or the power to bring those countries to task in regard to their commitments under GATT.
Are other countries thinking of getting together to form a world cartel in particular commodities, or is GATT going to be something like the International Monetary Fund under which you solemnly engage to abide by an agreement? As far as such agreements are concerned, I recall two or three different occasions on which Canada opted unilaterally for a floating exchange rate while everybody else was on a fixed exchange rate. We gained all the advantages. But what is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander. Unless some sanity is restored to international trade and some of these zonal or product cartels are suppressed, I foresee the world being in for a great deal of trouble.
I should like to have a report from the minister as to the general proposals Canada is going to adopt in the Tokyo negotiations, and whether there will be an enlargement of the cadre of the negotiators and teams who will be working at the conferences. Would the minister also outline the objectives Canada has in participating in these further rounds? How long does the minister expect them to last? I realize the minister will give what may be an uninformed guess, but at least it will give us the government's thinking on this point.
There is one item I want to raise in the absence of my colleague from Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) who has asked me to raise the point with the minister. The only time I can do it is on second reading, and since the item is absent from the bill I can only make representations at this time. It is a rather esoteric subject and one that would hardly be expected to loom large economically. Frankly, it
Customs Tariff
has to do with air conditioners in combine cabs. Yes, Mr. Speaker, they do exist. I dare say that in this day and age it is no longer necessary to have to work long hours, in extreme discomfort, in a combine in late July or August on the prairies where temperatures can get very high.
I might point out that tractor cab air conditioners are admitted under tariff item 40938-1. Air conditioner units are brought in from the United States, which is the sole economic source of supply, under, as I say, tariff item 40938-1, and there follows in brackets, "accessories not otherwise provided for". However, large-sized, self-propelled combines are similarly equipped with cabs and air conditioners. The air conditioners are subject to 15 per cent most favoured nation duty and 12 per cent excise tax. It appears that item 40916-1, which deals with thrashers and combines, does not provide for inclusion of excise as does item 40938-1. Recourse must then be taken under item 42700-1, which is the item in respect of machines generally not otherwise provided for. There is a right of application for remission of the duty, but if the importation is by an individual farmer there is little or no relief.
I have written to the minister, on behalf of my colleague and other members who have drawn this matter to my attention, asking why there should be this distinction in that air conditioners for tractor cabs are free of customs duty and sales tax whereas air conditioners for combines are not. This is a rather silly distinction. Surely the minister's officials to whom I have spoken about this matter are prepared to look into it to see if the situation can be corrected and the two items put on the same footing. Hopefully, this will not be accomplished by making them both subject to the 15 per cent imposition but, rather, they will be admitted free of duty.
I know that some of my colleagues have other points to raise in respect of this bill. This is a rather scattergun approach because we can go through items including bananas, melons, fish, herring, clams, sugar products, dehydrated citrus fruits, and many others. There may be particular points to be raised by some of my colleagues in respect of educational materials. I have been given to understand that there are some distinctions here which are not clear. These matters are of importance.
In any event, I hope that after discussion of this bill we can complete second reading and go into committee. With the hope that the parliamentary secretary will note the undertaking by the minister in respect of third reading, third reading can be postponed until tomorrow in order that we can get answers from the minister at that time. I do not foresee any great difficulty in the passage of this bill, but I think we should have this information on the record.

speakeroldname: Mr. Max Saltsman (Waterloo-Cambridge):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Customs Tariff ways and means bills are always interesting to look at, although I suspect there is generally not much interest in them from the public's point of view. In many ways they are outlines of changes in the government's policy and attitude. Customs Tariffs have been used since the beginning of Canadian history in this regard. Another feature of this bill is that it is loaded with all kinds of anomalies, as has been the case with bills of

January 22, 1975
Customs Tariff
this kind going back to confederation. One wonders why many items have continued to be subject to Customs Tariff for as long as they have. I have in mind two items that come in under the most favoured nation and Commonwealth preference. It may be that at some time in the 1800s someone in Canada was manufacturing cricket bats and the government decided to provide some protection, so cricket bats were made subject to tariff. This is now being changed and cricket bats will not be subject to any tariff provided they are brought in from a Commonwealth country.
Another item I have always been curious about is bananas. Why in the world we should have a tariff on bananas coming into Canada when, in fact, except under most extraordinary circumstances, we have no way of growing them here, is something that has escaped me. In attempting to get an answer to this question I asked the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) why we continued to have a tariff on bananas. He replied that there is competition in respect of different kinds of foods, and if people eat bananas they will not eat tomatoes-and we grow tomatoes here. In any event, I am glad to see that the tariff is coming off bananas.
In the past, Customs Tariffs have been used as instruments of combines policy. The royal commission report in the 1950s suggested that companies which colluded with each other in forming a combine against the public interest should be penalized by having their tariff protection removed. Since then two major cases have occurred, one in respect of the glass industry and the other in respect of the fine papers industry. In neither of those cases was the tariff removed. The companies were permitted to continue in operation, having been found guilty of collusion.
The interesting thing about this bill is that it represents a definite change in government attitude. Apparently the government is no longer worrying so much about industry but is more concerned with protecting the consumer. It is fairly obvious that the proposed changes are designed to lower prices to the consumer. This is in contrast to previous Customs Tariff bills. Certainly, in many ways it is a departure from government policy. To a very large extent, the government has in the past taken the position that it would not change tariffs because it wished to use them as negotiating tools in order to obtain concessions from other countries. By this bill it would seem the government has dropped this negotiating tool approach in favour of attempting to assist consumers. Even in this regard we find inconsistencies which illustrate the conflict which exists in government policy.
As an example, let us consider the situation regarding mobile homes. On the one hand we find that the mobile home industry in Canada is being protected by tariff provisions. When the government proposed the removal of excise tax on building materials, the proposal did not apply to mobile homes. This results in the fact that mobile homes are protected on the one hand and disadvantaged on the other, with the result that from two directions those who have a preference for mobile homes are penalized by having to pay higher prices than would normally be the case. Mobile homes represent an important aspect of housing in Canada, and as such are deserving of consideration. This situation will have to be straightened out

by the government. The industry is penalized on the one hand and rewarded on the other.
I suspect there is not a great deal of opposition to this bill. It does indicate the direction of government policy. Specifically, it indicates the government's concern regarding certain agricultural products-beef, for example. The government intended to remove some of the tariffs on processed beef. That intention was dropped because of the situation in Canada. There is still a substantial tariff in respect of sugar in spite of the fact that the sugar beet industry in Canada is not producing the volumes it once did when protection was required. It seems to me, the price of sugar being what it is, that the government might have removed the tariff on this commodity. I do not anticipate any difficulty in agreeing to the provisions of this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I will take a few minutes only to raise a question closely connected with Bill C-39, an Act to amend the Customs Tariff.
Recently the Cigar Tobacco Producers Association- representing producers not only from my constituency but producers across the country-asked me, through their secretary, to inquire whether the government intends to reduce duties on imported cigar tobacco.
Mr. Speaker, it will be immediately understood that Canadian producers of cigar tobacco are interested in maintaining adequate prices. If the government intends to reduce duties, clearly cigar manufacturers would welcome the opportunity to play competition with imported tobacco. I therefore contacted the department directly, only to learn that a study was underway on the subject. This caused a big disappointment to the Cigar Tobacco Producers Association, because the department implied that the cooperatives concerned had been informed of the proposition and that since they had made no representations or expressed any views, it was felt that these cooperatives would not oppose a reduction of custom duties on imported tobacco. Thanks to that association, a telegram was first quickly sent to the appropriate department to inform them that the cooperatives or producers concerned had not been informed of any such suggestion or recommendation as made by the cigar company.
I therefore think it is my duty to talk about those matters, since quite a few people in my constituency are concerned with that problem, and I think it is in the interest of every Canadian cigar tobacco producer to request from the minister a flat denial to that company which seeks lower tariffs on imported tobacco.
Still in the interest of Canadian producers and for their own protection and also in view of all the hard times our agriculture is going through, I don't think this is a very good time to put that category of producers in a difficult position.
I would therefore take advantage of this opportunity to increase the minister's awareness of that problem and ask him, on behalf of those producers, to say no to that cigar manufacturing company which would be extremely interested in lower customs tariffs.

Mr. Speaker, I hope these few remarks will prompt the minister to analyse thoroughly the extent of whatever step might be taken, considering in the first place the interest of Canadian producers. speakeroldname: Mr. Howard Johnston (Okanagan-Kootenay):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak on three different points involving the collection of customs at our borders. I agree with the points raised by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) who opened this debate, with one exception. There is rather keen public interest, I find, in the whole business of customs because there are a great many Canadians who pass back through our borders or who receive materials coming into Canada from outside.
During the short time that I have been back here, three specific points have been brought to my attention or have occurred to me, and I would like to raise them at this time. One is the question of duty on imported goods coming into western Canada, British Columbia specifically, from the United States and the fact that duty is applied although the goods in question are not manufactured in Canada and are not obtainable here. If the duty is to protect Canadian industry, that is one thing; but if there is no comparable Canadian industry, that is another matter.
The duty on goods that is designed specifically to protect Canadian manufacturers is suspect in western Canada where there is a long-standing feeling that many of the regulations regarding duties and imports were designed to protect central Canada at the expense of western Canada. So there is an exasperation even in connection with duty where it can be shown that the product is manufactured in Canada. If it cannot be shown that that is so, and attempts are made to find such a product in Canada but it is not possible to purchase it here and it is not necessary to protect a manufacturing process in Canada, and if then it is bought and paid for in the United States and on top of that a duty is charged, this certainly adds salt to the wound. It is one of the questions that I would like to raise. It was first raised with me during a recent visit to my constituency.
Another matter also came up and it is one that I find rather strange; that is, the duty charged on a specific class of gifts that enter the country. The specific category is
Customs Tariff
wedding gifts. Ours is not the only society in which it is more than customary to send wedding gifts; it is obligatory to send them. I think that is so, particularly if the couple involved are children or grandchildren of someone who lives far away on another continent. The happiness of the occasion is all too frequently marred by the arrival of unsolicited gifts that are perhaps even unexpected. But unexpected or not, the gifts arrive, necessitating a trip to the nearest Customs station-and that can be a trip of some miles in the interior of British Columbia-in order to pick up the gifts, only to find that the duty is so great that it amounts almost to buying the gifts.
With another kind of gift I suspect there would be a temptation to return them as having been unsolicited, and thus avoid the charge, but a wedding gift cannot be returned without causing a great deal of pain and anguish to the loving grandparents or the solicitous relatives who sent it. So there is really no alternative for the people in question except to pay the duty and to accept the gift and, hopefully, to say nothing about the duty when they thank the relative for sending the gift. Weddings, of course, are kept track of in this country: we have the Dominion Bureau of Statistics which insists on knowing when anyone is married in Canada. Also, licences are obtained and registers are signed. There is a very complex and complicated ritual to go through to prove that a wedding has taken place. So it seems to me that it would be a very simple matter for the Customs officials to ascertain that a wedding had taken place, and also I suspect it would be possible to set a limit at the upper end in order to avoid any unwise practices in the sending of very large and expensive gifts.
However, these are not really what I am talking about; I am talking about the kind of gift that is sent out of a warm heart or a love for absent children or grandchildren, which in turn may to them constitute an unexpected and, I feel, an unnecessary expense. It seems to me that any gift coming into the country, freely sent, of course adds to the country; nothing is lost. I do not feel the amount of revenue involved here would be very large, but the embarrassment, the pain and the surprise of finding that a gift sent on such an occasion is dutiable is something the government should seriously consider as unnecessary, and it should alter the Customs Tariff to take that particular, very limited and, as I say, very definable and traceable category of gifts off the list of dutiable items.
There is another area which I should like to discuss. It was mentioned in the parliamentary secretary's remarks. I refer to the decision to change the allowable value of items brought back into the country by a traveller who has been abroad for some time, and to raise it from $100 to $150. Here, again, there are all kinds of complexities involved in this decision. Why was the allowance raised at all? If there is sufficient justification to raise it, why only by $50? If it is going to be meaningful in today's world of rapid inflation, then surely it should have been raised to something like $500 rather than simply by $50. That will not help anything. If the situation needs some help, why not extend it to something genuine, such as to $300 or $500, a figure that would make sense-if it is going to be moved at all? If it is not just something to provide work for Customs

January 22, 1975
Customs Tariff
officials, who I find are pretty harried anyway and do not really need the extra work, then it should be raised substantially.
Of course, we have just been through an election campaign in which this country was told over and over again by members on the government side that inflation was worldwide and it was quite beyond the control of Canada to do anything about it. If the situation was truly so rampant and so outside our control, then it seems to me that this is one of the adjustments that should be taken into consideration in view of some of the remarks that were made during the election campaign. As I say, $50 is certainly no indication of the sort of situation that we were told over and over again was worldwide and which effectively prevented this government from taking any measures within the country to tackle what is certainly the most serious problem facing this nation, and probably the most serious it has ever faced.
There is another aspect of this matter which bothers me personally. I have travelled a fair amount and have come through Customs a good many times; I came through when the allowance was $100, and once during the period when it was increased to $200. If inflation is a problem within Canada, then I suppose when people travel outside this country and spend their money in other countries they are adding to the other country's inflation and not to our own. Perhaps we should encourage people to buy more when they are abroad because they will be hotting up the inflation in Europe, Japan or South America-wherever they are-and they will not be putting the same pressure on inflation in this country for the consumer goods they are purchasing outside. Maybe that is why it is proposed to raise the allowance from $100 to $150, although if that is the reason I think the increase is inadequate.
Quite apart from that, when I come back I read the little slip the Customs people give me-my wife and I always read these-and we fill out the two forms. The slip says "Declare everything", and so we do. We itemize our purchases and put everything down. I will never forget the irritation of the Customs official as I came back into the country and declared $114.90 as the value of the goods I was bringing with me. I had a very strong suspicion that he would have been delighted if I had changed my arithmetic at the last minute and declared $99.98, so that I could then have been whipped through the line with no trouble. But having done what I was told to do by the little card, I was given a variety of forms to be filled out and a variety of wickets to go to, and eventually there was a small cheque to write. I wonder, when the amount is raised so slightly, if it will not mean there will be some encouragement for people to declare $149.99 as the true value of the goods they are carrying with them.
So it seems to me that if there is to be a change at all- and I think there are several rather compelling reasons to make changes-it might as well be to a figure that would be more meaningful in today's inflationary world, rather than moving it from $100 to $150. That will be hardly worth the cost, plus the inflationary cost, of reprinting all the forms that will be necessary for the change. I am sure it will take a long time to collect from the extra $50 the revenue that will be needed just to pay for the changes in the forms.
As the bill is debated, I hope that the minister and the government will consider some amendments. I should like to see one in reference to wedding gifts that would remove what is, I think, in some ways an insulting and painful imposition on Canadians who receive gifts from relatives abroad such as parents and grandparents. Then there is the provision for a person bringing in goods from abroad valued at not more than $100. At least $100 is a good round figure, as would be $300 or $200, but to change it to $150 strikes me as an exercise in futility.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gordon Ritchie (Dauphin):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on this bill, which I do not think is a very controversial one. I agree with the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) that in the perennial argument on high tariffs and low tariffs, consumers are now being looked at somewhat more than they have in the past. Looking at conditions in the world and the apparent recession in the United States, which may be deepening, we may witness an increased desire on the part of other countries to ship manufactured goods and textiles to our market in an effort to earn foreign exchange and thus our own industries may exert pressure to be protected from low-cost imports in the next year or so. I hope this will be resisted within reason, although I concede it is difficult to find a solution when an industry in a particular area is being hammered by imports.
The government's policy of seeking greater trade with the European Common Market may be desirable, but we seem to be getting into trade hassles with the United States, our largest customer. This is something we have to consider, Mr. Speaker. We have had an example in the beef industry, where the effect of the application of quotas by both sides, and the DES ban, was probably greater than that of tariffs. I think the situation could have been avoided if both governments had used more good sense. The Canadian beef quota was imposed without much consultation with the industry or interested groups, but I think the American quota was imposed after they held hearings. I do not know if things would have been different if this country had held hearings first. The whole thing was handled poorly by both sides.
I should like to turn now to a specific problem, that of defining farm machinery for the purpose of the Customs Tariff. It seems to be the general understanding that this involves cases where farmers go across to the United States to buy a machine and bring it back here, expecting that it will be free of duty, only to find that duty is charged at the border. The problem arises when Customs officials decide that although the machine may be used on a farm, it may also be used somewhere else and is therefore liable for duty. In such cases the process of appeal is complicated and involved.
I know of one case where a man imported a machine on April 23, 1974, was charged duty, won his appeal, but is still waiting for the refund. Apparently the machine was designated as a multi-purpose dump wagon. Because of the word "wagon" it was defined not as a farm machine but as a general purpose machine by Customs officials, so he was charged duty, which he paid. The farmer appealed and the Customs official's decision was confirmed. The farmer

January 22, 1975

appealed to higher authority, and it was ruled that the dump wagon could in fact only be used as a farm machine, so he was entitled to a refund of the duty paid in May, 1974. He is still waiting for the refund.
I know this is a perennial question that members from the west have raised time and again. The procedures should be easier and quicker, and the final decision should not take so long. If a ruling is made in favour of the applicant, surely he should receive his refund reasonably quickly and the case closed.

speechtext: Order, please. Is the House ready for the question? The hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens).

speakeroldname: Mr. Sinclair Stevens (York-Simcoe):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before proceeding further with this bill, I believe it would be wise to draw to the attention of members of the House an item appearing in schedule 1. I do so because I believe that when we get into committee of the whole members will pay particular attention to this item, and I hope the hon. parliamentary secretary will have an explanation for us. I refer to tariff item 87500-1. As I read the item, it would appear that it is contemplated that handicraft goods designated by order of the governor in council, etc., may be exempted from, in most instances, all tariff under such regulations as the minister may prescribe. This appears to be a significant change from the customary way of handling Customs items as parliament, essentially, determines Customs and tariff levels. The cabinet has not been given power to designate items which shall enter duty free; at least, it has not been given the sort of power which is suggested in connection with the item to which I just referred.
As we know, this measure is to expire on June 30, 1976. Nevertheless, it constitutes a precedent which needs to be explained. While the term of the measure is relatively short, this precedent should not be set without adequate explanation. Parliament has the right and duty to legislate in the matter of Customs Tariffs, and in no way will it delegate that responsibility to the cabinet. The item in question is defined nebulously. I doubt whether you can designate handicrafts merely by an order of the governor in council, or say that the definition will be based on certain information which shall be received from various countries. The interpretation of what constitutes handicrafts may be extremely wide and may be subject to misuse later. Handicrafts have not been well defined and I should like to see the parliamentary secretary consider a tighter definition of the term. Unless the parliamentary secretary can show good cause for the inclusion of this item, I think the House ought to challenge it.

speakeroldname: Mr. Cullen:
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was under the impression that an hon. member was rising to speak. After the bill has been read the second time, we can discuss it clause by clause in committee of the whole. The minister will speak on third reading and will tell us, so far as he is able to, about the negotiations which are going on or are being contemplated in the area to which I previously referred. I noted the representations which the hon. member for Edmonton West made on behalf of the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski). He referred to tariff item 40916-1 and spoke of the difficulty in making application for remission. I have taken note of his representations and will bring them to the minister's attention.
The questions raised by the hon. member who spoke on behalf of the NDP were almost rhetorical. He asked a question and, in indicating procedures to be followed, suggested answers. I note with interest that the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) is not here at the moment, although I make nothing of that. The representations in question have been made; the co-ops sent telegrams. I will discuss that matter with the minister. According to my information, they had been made aware of the matter referred to. This will be checked into.
An hon. member raised the question of the import duty on goods not manufactured in Canada. He was not specific. If he can make specific reference to any particular case, perhaps I could bring it to the minister's attention. We could then look at the sorts of goods he has in mind. In all probability the kind of thing he is suggesting would need to be dealt with in the budget and considered by the House.
The hon. member who spoke about wedding gifts was concerned about a loophole in the law. I think the hon. member's arguments have merit, as I do not think great advantage can be taken of this provision. In this country one must do certain things before one can marry; therefore, the matter the hon. member has in mind can be looked into fairly easily.
Next I come to the matter of increasing to $150 the amount of goods which may be brought in, under certain conditions, duty free. As I said in my opening remarks, about four million items come into Canada under the $100 limit, and they represent about $110 million worth of goods. Raising the limit by $50 is a matter of judgment. I suppose one could push the limit up to $300, or even to $500 as the hon. member suggests, although the higher limit could damage, not help, those whom we want to help. I, too, have travelled abroad, as has the hon. member for Edmonton West. However, unlike him I did not have the money to bring back $150 worth of goods.

January 22, 1975
Customs Tariff
One of the last members who spoke suggested that this bill will be of benefit to consumers also. As more and more industries feel the pressure, they will want various tariff items to be re-imposed. This bill approaches these questions democratically. Under it, representations may be made, hearings held and consideration given to those representations. That is good. However, the consumer will not benefit if Canadian enterprises are driven out of business by competition from abroad. So there will be a dubious advantage if, because of reduced tariffs, cheaper goods come in from abroad. Such cheaper goods could drive Canadian manufacturing enterprises out of business and in the end we might have to pay more for those goods if they are obtainable only from outside the country. So this is a matter which must be considered.
The Department of National Revenue, which will have responsibility for administering this bill, will also be involved in its interpretation. Some of the points the hon. member referred to should be made to the Minister of National Revenue. The hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) questioned certain procedures under the bill. In my opening remarks I pointed out why certain procedures are being followed in the present instance. The number of handicrafts involved is not significant, and in any event it may be hard to define precisely what are handicrafts. We do not want to do this in such a way that we end up by bringing in more handicrafts to the detriment of Canadian enterprises. Of course, as I indicated in my opening remarks, the minister must be left with some discretion in order to ensure that our own craftsmen are not adversely affected by too broad an interpretation of "handicrafts." The present provision will decrease rather than increase the level of handicraft imports.
