speakeroldname: Mr. Lambert (Edmonton West):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there are a number of items on which we would like more information as to why they were included. I refer hon. members to page 4 of schedule 1. These are items which replace those stricken off by the effect of clause 1. We recognize many of these items as having been introduced in the May budget, but what is the motivation to make them free? Why should they be brought in free? I am looking at item 20612-1, bovine intranasal vaccines. We are not trying to be funny by referring to some of these items. They look rather complicated. The question is, in what volume do they move, and why is there any particular insistence on changing their category?
The next item to which I would refer is 42712-1, amusement riding devices of the kinds used at exhibitions or fairs, ancillary equipment imported therewith; parts of the foregoing. Why should these be entirely free, unless there is some question of their being part of a travelling circus

or amusement fair such as the royal American shows which have two strings travelling throughout western Canada. One visits the Calgary Stampede and the Edmonton exhibition, or Klondike Days, and the other goes to Saskatoon, Regina and perhaps Winnipeg. Perhaps that is the case here; I do not know.
There is an extension of that. I know I am getting rather quizzical looks about this, but I heard about two years ago that 44043-1 would be closed off and some terminal date put on it, rather than yearly extensions. These are aircraft and aircraft engines, ancillary item 44047-1. Every year, in every budget, the terminal date is changed. I now go to item 69615-1. Some of my colleagues might be interested in this. It is primarily moving picture films, sound recordings, video tape recordings, wall charts, maps and posters of an educational, scientific or cultural character. There is a change from the original definition. I would like the parliamentary secretary to advise if there is an expansion as a result of the introduction of subparagraph (a) for this particular item. Is there greater precision as to the nature of this material? I know we have had problems with this in the past. The parliamentary secretary will get my list of these at the end.

speakeroldname: Mr. Cullen:
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I was going to say it is.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lambert (Edmonton West):
speechtext:
The next item, 69645-1, represents sound recordings in single copies which are sent merely to reviewers. This has caused problems in the past. It is a move in the right direction. On second reading I spoke about the changes in items 70310-1, 70311-1, 70312-1 and 70313-1 with regard to tourists. However, I want to deal with item 87500-1 which was referred to by the hon. member for Simcoe. He, quite rightly, indicated that the designation of goods under this item is usually by order in council and may be varied by order in council, which is a departure from the normal Customs Tariff procedure. I have never seen anything like this in the whole of the Customs Tariff. I thought I detected among some of the officials a bit of disagreement with my colleague on that point. I want to know precisely what we are moving into with this type of operation.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was good enough, in informal discussion, to remind me of this; but I recall in 1962, at the time of a financial crisis, the then government moved to shift certain goods from one item to a higher category, working together with the forgiveness clause in the Financial Administration Act. There was great legal controversy about that. The government was actually moving commodities from one item to another within the tariff, and that is not authorized. In 18 years experience with budgets, it has always been my impression-certainly I have always been told this by officials of the Department of National Revenue and by Customs officials of the Department of Finance-that in order to add a particular item, and the air conditioners which I spoke about is precisely one such item, it has to be done as the result of a formal change in the Customs Tariff.
A formal change in the Customs Tariff can only come about through a finance bill following the presentation of a budget or a ways and means motion. In other words, it is
January 22, 1975

then formally out in the open. But this language clearly indicates that we are giving to the administration a completely free hand-I do not care what the motivation is; the motivation may be fine-to widen as much as possible the entry into Canada of handicraft goods from countries entitled to the benefits of the preferential tariff. We know that these countries are developing countries, but why is the House in this instance being asked to give the governor in council the power by order to add or subtract the number or types of these goods? Unless I am wrong, this does not appear in any other item in the Customs Tariff. I think it would be a dangerous precedent to ask the House on this occasion to grant authority to the governor in council to change the Customs Tariff, not by setting quotas, as is already provided for, or as to how goods are to be brought in under regulation, but as to what goods and from what country shall be allowed in free.
If this were done, we would again be confronted with very innocent looking wording in an item asking for the same power in relation to another category of goods. Therefore, the House's authority over the Customs Tariff would be further eroded. It does not matter whether we have in existence a committee on statutory instruments to review these matters; this committee cannot touch an order in council or a statutory instrument as to its merit. It may see that it is legal, that it is within the power of the governor in council to make the order, and so forth, but that is all.
I say to members of this House, as we have in the past, that the authority of this chamber is being eroded more and more. Every time we pass legislation making general provisions regarding orders in council, we are just wrapping the rope around our ankles one more turn. It all sounds very nice and complacent, and government members are prepared to accept it because their master shall tell them to do so. But I already know that some of them are feeling restive at the fact that these innocuous phrases are used with devastating effect on later occasions, and that the practice is continuing. It is a matter of administrative convenience, but I must say that one can pay a very high price for so-called administrative convenience and efficiency.
So, Madam Chairman, I hope we will get from the parliamentary secretary a satisfactory explanation of this item. If he feels that he is not in a position to do so, then we should stand this clause and await the return of the minister tomorrow, who, of course, has the power to make decisions, to amend or to give undertakings. As far as I am concerned, I am not prepared to accept the passage of this particular item in schedule I as it appears and as I have understood it.

speakeroldname: Mr. Cullen:
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, the first item raised by the hon. member was item 20612-1. My information is that this is a new item which will provide duty free entry for bovine intranasal vaccines used to treat respiratory diseases in cattle. Similar bovine vaccines which are administered by injection are free of duty. The intranasal vaccines are administered by means of a spray, for the information of hon. members opposite. I understand these vaccines are made in Canada only by Connaught Laboratories Limited of Willowdale, Ontario, and they do not object to the duty free entry being provided in this area. Like others, I
Customs Tariff
wondered how these were administered, and I understand that it is by means of a spray.
With regard to item 42712-1 having to do with amusement rides, again this is a new item providing for free entry for amusement riding devices of a kind used at exhibitions. The item also covers related equipment imported with the rides. The duties on most amusement rides are remitted under the machinery program since they are not available from Canadian manufacturers. Rides not dealt with under the machinery program are dutiable at various rates, depending on the nature of each ride.
With regard to the import aspect, detailed figures are not available but the total is estimated at between $1 million and $2 million annually, and about one-third of these will be dealt with under the machinery program. Most of the duty on the equipment imported by foreign midways servicing Canadian fairs is remitted under the amusement riding devices remission order. Examples of rides covered by this new item are merry-go-rounds, ferris wheels, boat rides, car and train rides, and most roller coasters. Coin operated amusement devices and playground equipment are not covered by the item.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lambert (Edmonton West):
speechtext:
Could I interject a question here? Would this item in any way assist Canadian operations in the setting up of exhibition packages of the kind you see at the Central Canadian Exhibition here, so we would not have to rely upon big American operations like the royal American shows? Canadian operators would, of course, have a much more limited use of these items.
I would also ask whether there is an expansion of what one might call stationary amusement grounds. In some cities you have municipally-operated playgrounds and parks which more and more are using amusement rides, and I am wondering whether these operators would be assisted. Of course, the fact that they come in duty free means that they will never be manufactured in Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Cullen:
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. member is correct. The main reason for this item is to facilitate Canadian operators. Just what impact it may or may not have is a question of judgment or conjecture, but most assuredly it has been done to facilitate Canadian operators at municipal or private exhibitions.

speakeroldname: The Assistant Deputy Chairman:
speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Dauphin.

speakeroldname: Mr. Cullen:
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, might I just finish dealing with the matters raised by the hon. member for Edmonton West? With regard to item 44043-1 and item 44047-1, the hon. member asked why we were retaining these items. We are doing so on a temporary basis in order to facilitate possible future negotiations. We felt that this protection had to be given. I also have a comment to make on tariff item 69615-1. Rather than trying to summarize it, I think possibly I should read it into the record and then it will be before hon. members. This item was established to carry out Canada's obligation assumed under UNESCO agreement for facilitating the international circulation of visual and auditory materials of an educational, scientific
2522

January 22, 1975
Customs Tariff
and cultural character, more generally known as the Beirut convention.
Under the item as it is now drafted, the Department of National Revenue, Customs and Excise, has no choice but to accept entry under the item of any of the audio-visual goods specified in the item if they have been certified in accordance with the convention to be of educational, scientific or cultural character. The convention provides that the final authority to decide whether any imported product should be accorded the duty free entry privilege contemplated by the convention rests with-and this is in quotation marks because it comes from the convention- "an appropriate governmental agency" of the importing country.
The proposed amendment is designed to permit the Department of National Revenue to exercise that authority. It has become necessary to give this authority to Canadian Customs because some of the certifying agencies of other state parties to the convention have become somewhat lax about issuing certifications. Postcards picturing Canadian scenery, cities, monuments, etc., printed abroad and imported for resale to the tourist trade have been certified. This gives you some indication of the laxity or tendency to laxity, and that is the reason for this particular section. I understand a movie picture film showing car salesmen how to sell a particular make of automobile has been certified. These are products which were clearly not contemplated by the convention. However, because they have been certified by a designated agency in the country of production, they must be allowed duty free under this item at the present time. Producers of competitive goods within Canada are at a double disdvan-tage since goods allowed duty free entry under item 69615-1 are also exempt from federal sales tax, while the Canadian-made product is not exempt.

speakeroldname: Mr. Kempling:
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, I have a question for the parliamentary secretary on this item. I understand what the parliamentary secretary is trying to get at in this regard, but I had a particular example of this on an advertisement that came into my business office, not my office in parliament. This advertisement dealt with a rather delicate subject. In other quarters we might call it a girlie film. At any rate, it dealt with tape cassettes showing nude women in various poses and positions. This material was also available in the form of slide films. On the top of the advertisement there was a typewritten piece of paper which read, "This has been approved by Canadian Customs as educational material". This rather shocked me, as I am not in the educational business but, rather, in the machinery business. Clearly, this material was being advertised for companies to show at business conventions, and so forth.
I first wrote to the Postmaster General as this material came to me through the mail. Much to my surprise, I received a reply from one of the Postmaster General's executive assistants, who happens to be a woman, saying that she was shocked as well but this material had been ruled educational by the Customs people. I am wondering just how far this sort of thing goes.

I am not a "square", by any stretch of the imagination, but I must say it was very embarrassing to have this sort of thing come into my office and circulate among the young people there. I can see this going into a psychiatrist's or gynecologist's office or something like that, but certainly not into the average business office. I am wondering whether the parliamentary secretary could tell us if these films are submitted to Customs and Excise people, and whether in fact they have ruled that they are educational. Also, are the people mailing this sort of material into Canada legally allowed to state in the advertising that the material is admissible as educational material by Customs?

speakeroldname: Mr. Cullen:
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Madam Chairman, the hon. member is not a "square", because he obviously viewed the film before he criticized it.

speakeroldname: Mr. Kempling:
speechtext: I just read the advertisement; I did not see the film.

speakeroldname: Mr. Cullen:
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is fine. You have done your duty as a good citizen, and I compliment you for that. It is specifically for this reason that this section is put in here. This was not approved by the Customs for educational purposes, but was approved by the country of origin using the rules under the convention to indicate it was for that purpose. That is an indication of the laxity to which I have referred. Canadian Customs, under the convention, would have no alternative if the sending country had approved it. They would simply be admitting what the sending country obviously felt was educational. Perhaps the film was educational, if the hon. member did not see it, and perhaps there is something we could learn together from it.

speakeroldname: Mr. Kempling:
speechtext: I gather, from the way this rule is applied, that we would be allowed to send the same type of material into the United States, specifically California- from where this advertisement came-if we classified it as educational material.

speakeroldname: Mr. Cullen:
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes. Specifically, that is where the decision would be made in this country. If that particular film were to be moved from our country to another country under the convention, we would not be so lax as to give that kind of approval. At least, that would be my judgment.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lambert (Edmonton West):
speechtext: The important thing in this situation is that power should be given to Department of National Revenue officials to make their own designation as to whether it is for educational purposes and to countermand, shall we say, the lax operations of the country of origin. Otherwise, quite frankly, there would be no benefit. It is bad enough to import somebody else's smut, but to balance it we should not have to export smut or pornography, or whatever you want to call it. We should not, in turn, send such material back as educational material. It might educate some people, but not exactly in the way we might want.

speakeroldname: Mr. Cullen:
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
That is specifically why we have this section. From our point of view such smut or material is unacceptable as educational material and we would find an appropriate term whereby it would not be permitted as
January 22, 1975

an export to some other country. The next item raised by the hon. member has to do with a whole series of items dealing with what has been called, I suppose for want of a better name, the tourist exemption. These are the items which allow Canadian residents returning from trips abroad to import goods without payment of duties and taxes, or to pay such duties and taxes if they do not meet the conditions for exemption at a single, combined rate.
The changes being proposed are as follows: the quarterly exemption available after a 48-hour absence is doubled to $50 from $25; the annual exemption is being increased to $150 from $100 and will be made available after an absence of seven days, instead of 12; the over-all amount of goods which may be cleared at the flat rate of 25 per cent is being increased from $100 to $150; and, finally, the $5 casual exemption is being increased to $10. Having regard to the 25 per cent flat rate, most consumer goods purchased by travellers would otherwise be subject to Customs duty, sales and excise taxes of at least 25 per cent of the retail value. Duty free imports by returning Canadian residents, as I indicated earlier, amounted to $110 million in 1973, of which about $71.6 million were from the United States.
Judging from the hon. member's comments, he is most critical of those sections thus far objected to by the hon. member for York-Simcoe. Here again, this is not something new as there is already provision under the Customs Tariff Act for withdrawal, for example, of a general preferential tariff. May I say, for the edification of all hon. members, that this can be found in the Customs Tariff Act, section 3(2), and I refer specifically to subsection 2 where the governor in council may, by order in council, from time to time withdraw the benefit of the general preferential tariff in whole or in part from any country to which it has been extended. That would answer the hon. member who, I think appropriately enough, does not wish to see authority drain away from parliament.
What we have tried to do in this instance is see to it that something does not come into the country that we want to restrict. I could name, off the top of my head, things like Eskimo carvings from another country and the impact they would have. It is a handicraft, but we want to be able to say it is not a handicraft within the meaning of this section. I do not know whether or not this is an example of giving one more turn to the rope around the ankles, as was mentioned by the hon. member.
I might say that this item will provide for duty free entry of handicraft products from developing countries, that is, countries which have been designated as beneficiaries under the general preferential tariff. A list of handicraft products to be allowed entry under this item will be established by order in council. An initial list of such products could include wood carvings, basketwork, ceramic articles, pottery, jewellery, glassware, batik prints, shawls, scarves and mufflers. I am happy that my wife has taken up batiking; otherwise I would not have known how to pronounce the word.
For many products it may be difficult to distinguish between handicrafts and other products simply on the basis of their technical and physical characteristics. It is
Customs Tariff
therefore necessary to require certification by a competent authority in the exporting country. So that here again I suspect it is a question of degree. The hon. member for York-Simcoe pointed out that this is a temporary measure covering a particular area. I think it is right to raise it, but it may be making too big a bogey out of this particular operation.

speakeroldname: Mr. O'Connell:
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, I do not think you saw me rise because I am behind you. May I ask the parliamentary secretary a few questions on item 69615-1? First, these items are now shown as being free of duty. What was the tariff prior to this change? Second, does the convention require that the items described here enter Canada free of duty, or is it in the discretion of the importing country to establish a tariff item and, if so, are there limitations?
Third, I would like to ask whose designation prevails in the case when it is a question of whether the item, such as a moving picture film, a video tape recording, and so forth, fits these categories. Is it the importing country, that is, Canada in our case, or is it sufficient for the exporting country to so designate, or is it the United Nations? If it is only one of these, what arrangements are there for resolving any differences of opinion as to whether an item fits a category or not? Are there such arrangements? What are the arrangements with the provinces with respect to educational-cultural designations?
Finally, I should like to ask the parliamentary secretary, without unduly complicating his life at this point, the following question. This convention was established in 1948, as I read in the report here. Do we in Canada have many difficulties with the convention that have come to his attention, and if we do, is there any pressure on our part to have it reviewed?

speakeroldname: Mr. Cullen:
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I thank the hon. member for his question. Quite frankly, I did not consider, in answer to the question raised, the previous form of the tariff. As the hon. member indicated, either in the late 1940s or early 1950s, since the convention was adopted, these goods have come in free of duty. The convention provides that they come in free of duty, and there is no discretion allowed the host country. Once you sign the convention, the products must come in free.

speakeroldname: Mr. O'Connell:
speechtext: There is no change here, is there?

speakeroldname: Mr. Cullen:
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No. The main purpose of this provision is to give the Department of National Revenue the authority, which it does not have now, to stop entry of the kind of product mentioned by the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth. There is an appeal procedure if a question does arise as to whether an item should or should not have been accepted under the convention. The convention applies to these procedures.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ritchie:
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, I should like to put a question regarding tourist exemptions. A year or two ago, in discussions with the United States with regard to trade, the so-called tourist exemption provisions came in for considerable discussion and the question was raised whether or not this was a trade irritant. At that time it appeared that the Americans felt we discriminated unrea-
2524

Customs Tariff
sonably against Canadians bringing back goods, mainly from the United States, compared with their nationals. I should like to ask the parliamentary secretary what discussions, if any, there have been with the United States authorities. Second, what effect will the exemptions which are now in effect have on our balance of payments or the relative value of pay-out from tourists back in Canada, versus Americans going home from Canada?

speakeroldname: Mr. Cullen:
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I might say to the hon. member that I tried to indicate the amount of money involved, the number of Canadians and the amount spent by Canadians, which is roughly the same, although I am advised by officials that Americans now spend more in Canada. This move was not made after consultation but was a unilateral move by Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ritchie:
speechtext: Could the parliamentary secretary give any indication as to what effect this new ruling will have on the relative spending of these two groups of tourists in each other's country? Have any such calculations been made?

speakeroldname: Mr. Cullen:
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I understand that this matter has been studied and there are some figures which I may give when the officials have them. We do not have them here, but I shall provide them to the hon. member.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ritchie:
speechtext: I have a question which relates to a bicycle factory at Rivers, Manitoba, which the hon. member for Marquette raised. There was a combined effort by Japanese interests and the Department of Northern Affairs and Indian Development to attempt to involve some of our native people. There was some complaints that the tariff changes would cause much hardship and perhaps the closing of the factory. I believe that the minister, along with the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, undertook to look into this matter to see whether the complaint was justified and whether any other arrangements could be made. Could the parliamentary secretary give an answer to this question?

speakeroldname: Mr. Cullen:
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Yes. Meetings have been held with this industry and with others in a similar industry. My information is that officials in the department and other interested government departments met with Canadian bicycle manufacturers and asked for further information from them. The additional information which has now been received from the manufacturers is being reviewed, and I understand that the minister's officials will be reporting to him shortly on this item. If any change is proposed there is authority to withdraw this provision by order in council.
Some meetings have already been held, but they need more. I understand the information is now in and the officials are to bring it to the attention of the minister. My information is that there is no particular dispute, as I think is alleged in the press, between the departments. It is a matter that they are concerned with and that they are both looking at.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ritchie:
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, on the matter of tariffs on sugar and rice, sugar of course has risen rapidly in

price. There have been many consumer complaints, but it would seem that sugar prices will remain relatively high. As I understand it, our sugar industry is protected by a subsidy when there are abnormally low prices. I believe it is a national decision whether or not we have a sugar industry, because the cost of producing sugar in Canada has been very much higher than outside. With this in mind, I was asked what advantage there would be in having a sugar tariff at this time. Even more so in the case of rice, it would seem in the interests of the consumer and of Canada as a whole that rice be admitted duty free. It is hard to see what industries would be adversely affected by the addition of rice as a duty free product.

speakeroldname: Mr. Cullen:
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. member is dealing with clause 2. I wonder if we should finish the items in clause 1 first, and we will then go into the item raised by the hon. member.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stevens:
speechtext:
I would ask the parliamentary secretary to return to his explanation of item 87500-1. I believe he gave a precedent. I did not have the advantage of seeing the wording of the tariff item that he was referring to, or the section, but as I understand his remarks there seemed to be discretionary power given to the cabinet to withdraw an item if they saw fit. I believe that is considerably different from the provision we are being asked to pass today, which is going the other way in giving the cabinet the right to include certain handicraft items as they see fit.
I raise this question because I think the wording of 87500-1 is very wide. As I read it, the country from which Canada is importing these handicrafts simply designates what goods should be included as handicrafts. In that way they can take advantage of the section that we are passing which in turn, as I read it, is a straight delegation of authority by this parliament to cabinet to take this action. I was wondering if the parliamentary secretary could be more explicit and indicate whether he has any precedent for the cabinet being given the power to include certain goods not already set out in a tariff schedule in the fashion that has been contemplated under 87500-1.

speakeroldname: Mr. Cullen:
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: My information is that under section 273 of the Customs Act there is provision to designate materials that can be either reduced or removed, and this reference is specifically to goods to be further processed. I believe this is the precedent to which the hon. member referred.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stevens:
speechtext: Could the parliamentary secretary indicate if those items are actually shown in the tariff? I think there is a distinction between saying that the cabinet has the right to say that item such and such may be reduced or otherwise dealt with under the schedule-its being mentioned by name-but here we have a broad concept of simply referring to handicraft goods, and I would like to know the precedent for that type of broad power being given by parliament to cabinet to deal, in a discretionary way, with what shall come under the heading of handicraft goods.

speakeroldname: Mr. Cullen:
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
There seems to be some suggestion that that does not appear. I am informed that it is under section 273, paragraphs (j), (k) and (1). If there is some concern about this item and hon. members wish to stand it, we could do
so.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lambert (Edmonton West):
speechtext:
On this particular point, clause 273 does not appear in the Customs Tariff Act because there are not that many clauses, but if one goes to the Customs Act I would agree that there is a clause 273. It is headed "Powers of the governor in council". But in the revised statutes there is quite a distinction; there is a transfer of materials to lists of free entry provided they are used in articles of Canadian manufacture. Handicraft goods are not; they are already finished. So they are different. Paragraph (k) reads:
-Granting a drawback of the whole or part of the duty paid on articles that have been used in Canadian manufacture-
Paragraph (i) reads:
-regulating the form in which transfers of goods in warehouse or bond from one person to another shall be entered-
Paragraph (j) refers to materials that enter into the manufacture of Canadian articles, Canadian manufactures. This is not just a matter of goods being brought in and then sold. As a matter of fact, it is very interesting to see the type of regulations that the governor in council can make under section 273 of the Customs Act. They are not of the type that is contemplated in this particular item. The parliamentary secretary was correct that the governor in council in many instances, under the Customs Tariff, has the power of making orders in council or regulations as to the manner in which goods may be imported. Certainly, the Minister of Finance under certain sections of the act has the power of setting a quota with regard to any particular commodity, and it is done by order in council. I am in full agreement there. But again I come to the point that this is a precedent for the adding or the subtraction of commodities which are handicraft items. Eskimo carvings, for example, could be produced cheaply, machine-made, but certainly they would not be handicrafts within the description of this item.
I rather think the parliamentary secretary will want to recast his thinking on this particular item. I would agree with his suggestion that this item in clause 1 should stand because of the discussion that has arisen. It can be dealt with later by the minister. I think that if we stood the item we could deal with schedule 2 and clauses 2 and 3, then stand the bill for further consideration of clause 1 in committee of the whole. The committee could then rise and report progress, and perhaps we could see it as six o'clock.

speakeroldname: Mr. Haidasz:
speechtext: I would like to ask the parliamentary secretary, with regard to tariff item 87500-1, whether the handicraft goods referred to in that item would include imported national costumes and rare musical instruments that many ethnic cultural dance and song and musical ensembles have to import into Canada from other countries. Since the multiculturalism program was announced by the government there has been increased interest in these cultural functions, and many of these people have had to pay higher duties on national costumes and musical instruments of a rare kind which are not available in Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lambert (Edmonton West):
speechtext:
They cannot come in under the general preferential tariff?
Customs Tariff

speakeroldname: Mr. Cullen:
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am advised that provided they met the definition, it is conceivable that they could. We are talking about goods coming in from developing countries and it has to be the general preferential tariff. I draw that caveat to the attention of the hon. member. I do not want to confuse him and say any country could do that, but conceivably these items come within the definition that would make it possible. I thank him for the question.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roche:
speechtext: Madam Chairman, with reference to item 87500-1 I want to ask the parliamentary secretary if this is the main way in which we would import handicraft items from developing countries, in view of the statements by the minister in the budget that such imports would be increased. If so, what would be the approximate trade value of those importations? If all this is aimed at meeting our trade relations with developing nations in an effort to have them plug into the international trade systems of the world in a more meaningful way, what are the criteria for the selection of those developing countries that we wish to help? Which developing countries would benefit most from the specific item we are discussing now?

speakeroldname: Mr. Cullen:
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Madam Chairman, I am given to understand that well over 100 countries have been proclaimed to qualify under this provision. I should like to say to the hon. member that this is a small or insignificant factor. The whole series, reducing tariff items on goods coming in from developing countries, became effective on July 1.

speakeroldname: Mr. Johnston:
speechtext: Madam Chairman, could I return to item No. 70313-1? I should like to know how long this amount has remained at $100? During the years it has gone up to $200, but I do not know whether it has gone below $100. For how many years has it stood at $100?

speakeroldname: Mr. Cullen:
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Madam Chairman, while officials are looking up those figures, might I reply to a question asked by the hon. member for Dauphin? In 1971 the over-all balance with the United States, in Canada's favour, was $194 million; in 1972, $104 million; and in 1973, the first half, $77 million. In reply to the question of the hon. member for Okanagan-Kootenay, the allowance has been $100 since 1970.

speakeroldname: Mr. Johnston:
speechtext: Was it raised, or lowered, in 1970? Had it been a higher, or a lower, figure?

speakeroldname: Mr. Cullen:
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It was raised.

speakeroldname: Mr. Johnston:
speechtext:
I still wonder at the reason for this figure. Is the purpose to reduce Canadian spending overseas, or is it related at all to trade deficits? In the parliamentary secretary's earlier reply he mentioned that it had something to do with the total value of goods that came into the country without duty because of this provision. I am wondering why we continue to impose it; why we allow this advantage. If we were running a heavy trade deficit, I should think this might be a factor in an effort to reduce Canadian spending overseas. As I have observed the pressure of traffic at airports in recent times, however, I wonder whether the government might not be under some pressure from Customs officials. When a giant plane comes in, you can see them turn pale at the prospect of all

January 22, 1975
Customs Tariff
these instant decisions. If that has anything to do with it, it seems to me that a higher figure might make sense.

speakeroldname: Mr. Cullen:
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I might say, first of all, that I was using the figure as an illustration to give some indication to the House of the number of people and the amount of money involved. Secondly, when I was given the earlier figures I believe I said for the first half of 1973 it was $77 million. I should have said that was an estimate. Over-all we are running a deficit on tourist expenditures of $202 million for 1971, $234 million for 1972, and the estimate for 1973 is $290 million. I do not believe it was a question of penalty; I think it was a question of an additional exemption for tourists, an accommodation to them rather than a penalty. If we were attempting to cut down their expenditure, we might move the figure the other way. It is a question of judgment whether we put it at $170, $125 or $200. This figure seems reasonable in the circumstances, and it will be watched.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lambert (Edmonton West):
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, as I count it, it is only of 18 months and a bit duration. It is designed as a temporary spur to the importation, primarily from the Caribbean and developing countries, of certain foodstuffs, raw materials, sugar, animal products and fruits. I do not know just how much it will stimulate the importation of goods from those countries against importation from traditional sources. Perhaps we could get an indication from the parliamentary secretary as to the real motivation and why it is only for 18 months. The former rates, particularly in the general tariff, will apply to those commodities once we reach June, 1976. The list is a bit esoteric and varied. The parliamentary secretary might also indicate, for the benefit of some of my colleagues, how
and why certain terms are chosen, because the list appears rather strange and it is a very mixed bag.

speakeroldname: Mr. Cullen:
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Madam Chairman, I am advised that this is part of our anti-inflationary move. That is why tariffs are reduced. This does not apply only to Caribbean and developing countries, although some foodstuffs come only from such places. As for definitions, these are consumer products. I suspect that the list is made up as products are exported to this country. The list is probably extended from time to time as particular consumer products come on the market.
